# Residuals {data-stack-name="Residuals"}


## How residuals work

::::: panel-tabset

### The gist
::: card-list-center

- Residuals = Estimated "errors" from our predicted model.

- $\text{Data} =  \underbrace{\text{Slope} \times x + \text{Intercept}}_\text{Predicted Line} + \text{Residuals}$

- $\text{Residuals} = \text{Data} - \text{Predicted Line}$

:::

```{=html}

<div style="height:200px"></div>

```

### Illustration

![](/assets/regression_to_residuals.gif){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Residuals = Data - Predicted Line"}

### Implication

What can residuals tell us about our predicted model?

- The estimated "errors" from our predicted model are called residuals.
    - Since the true errors are random (by definition), if our predicted model is correct, the residuals should also be random.

<!--

### Slightly more accurate

$y_\text{model} = \text{intercept}_\text{model} + \text{slope}_\text{model} \times x_\text{data points}$

$y_\text{data points} =  y_\text{model} + \text{errors}_\text{model}$

$\text{errors}_\text{model} = y_\text{data points} - y_\text{model}$

-->

::::::

## Getting residuals with `lm()`
The `lm()` function in R automatically calculates the residuals for you. 

```r
predicted_model <- lm(... ~ ..., data = ...)
residuals <- predicted_model$residuals
residuals
```

```{r}
model1 <- lm(reported_shape ~ hours, data = data1)
residuals <- model1$residuals
residuals
```

## Residual plots

```r
data <- data %>% mutate(residudals = predicted_model$residuals)
ggplot(data=data, aes(x=..., y=residuals)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")
```

```{r}
#| fig-align: "center"

data1 <- data1 %>% mutate(resids = model1$residuals)

ggplot(data=data1, aes(x=hours, y=resids)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", color = "firebrick")

```

Because residuals are noise, they should look random (no slope or pattern). Something is likely wrong with the analysis if the residuals don't look random (slope is 0).


## 

Compare these plots plots.

:::: columns
::: {.column .nonincremental}

**Dataset 1: Reported shape vs. hours**

```{r}

ggplot(data=data1, aes(x=hours, y=reported_shape)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm") + labs(title="Regression")

```

```{r}

data1 <- data1 %>% mutate(resids = model1$residuals)

ggplot(data=data1, aes(x=hours, y=resids)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", color = "firebrick") + labs(title="Residuals")

```

:::

::: {.column .nonincremental}

**Dataset 2: Heart rate vs. hours**

```{r}

data2 <- read_csv("./data/bpmVsHours.csv")
ggplot(data=data2, aes(x=hours, y=bpm)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm") + labs(title="Regression")

```

```{r}

model2 <- lm(bpm ~ hours, data=data2)
data2 <- data2 %>% mutate(resids = model2$residuals)

ggplot(data=data2, aes(x=hours, y=resids)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", color = "firebrick") + labs(title="Residuals")

```

:::
::::

## Interpretation

::: nonincremental

- We can see that in the second dataset, there is still a pattern in the residual plot. Specifically, there is an clear curve in residuals. This means that the straight line model that we have fitted to the data is not accounting for all systematic variance. Ideally, we want a model that can capture the true relationship between two variables, so a better model should be chosen to account for more of the systematic patterns. When our chosen model is more similar to the true model, the residuals should appear more randomly scattered.

:::

# Polynomial curve fitting {data-stack-name="Polynomial curve fitting"}

## Fitting curved lines using polynomials

:::::: columns
::::: {.column .nonincremental}

::: nonincremental
- Order 1: $y \sim x$
- Order 2: $y \sim x^2$
- Order 3: $y \sim x^3$
:::

:::::

::::: {.column .nonincremental}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10

x = seq(0, 10, by = 0.01)

`y = x` <- x

`y = x^2` <- x^2

`y = x^3` <- x^3

poly <- tibble(x=x, `y = x`=`y = x`, `y = x^2` = `y = x^2`, `y = x^3` = `y = x^3`)

poly <- poly %>% pivot_longer(names_to = "order", values_to = "y", cols = c(2,3,4))

ggplot(data=poly, aes(x=x, y=y, color = order)) + geom_line() + ylim(0,100)

```

:::::

::::::

## 

:::::: panel-tabset

## `poly()` function

::: nonincremental
- Fits a model with an order 1 polynomial
    - 
        
        ```r
        lm(data$y ~ poly(data$x, 1))
        ```
    - Equivalent are standard regression models

- Fits a model with an order 2 polynomial
    - 

        ```r
        lm(data$y ~ poly(data$x, 2))
        ```

:::

```{=html}
<div style="height:100px"></div>

```

## Plotting a curved line

```r
ggplot(data=data2, aes(x=..., y=...)) + geom_point() + 
    geom_smooth(method="lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2))
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4

ggplot(data=data2, aes(x=hours, y=bpm)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2))

```

## Straight line plots

:::::: panel-tabset

## Model fit plots

```{r}
library(patchwork)

data1 <- read_csv("./data/shapeVsHours.csv")
data2 <- read_csv("./data/bpmVsHours.csv")
data3 <- read_csv("./data/prodVsHours.csv")

plot1 <- ggplot(data1, aes(x=hours,y=reported_shape)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

plot2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x=hours,y=bpm)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

plot3 <- ggplot(data3, aes(x=hours,y=productivity)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")


model1 <- lm(reported_shape ~ hours, data = data1)
model2 <- lm(bpm ~ hours, data = data2)
model3 <- lm(productivity ~ hours, data = data3)

data1 <- data1 %>% mutate(resids = model1$residuals)
data2 <- data2 %>% mutate(resids = model2$residuals)
data3 <- data3 %>% mutate(resids = model3$residuals)

resids1 <- ggplot(data1, aes(x=hours,y=resids)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

resids2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x=hours,y=resids)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

resids3 <- ggplot(data3, aes(x=hours,y=resids)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

plot1 + plot2 + plot3

```

## Residual plots

```{r}

resids1+resids2+resids3

```

::::::

## 2nd order plots

:::::: panel-tabset

## Model fit plots

```{r}
model1.2 <- lm(data1$reported_shape ~ poly(data1$hours, 2))
model2.2 <- lm(data2$bpm ~ poly(data2$hours, 2))
model3.2 <- lm(data3$productivity ~ poly(data3$hours, 2))

data1 <- data1 %>% mutate(resids2 = model1.2$residuals)
data2 <- data2 %>% mutate(resids2 = model2.2$residuals)
data3 <- data3 %>% mutate(resids2 = model3.2$residuals)

plot1.2 <- ggplot(data1, aes(x=hours,y=reported_shape)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula = y ~ poly(x,2))

plot2.2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x=hours,y=bpm)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula = y ~ poly(x,2))

plot3.2 <- ggplot(data3, aes(x=hours,y=productivity)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula = y ~ poly(x,2))

resids1.2 <- ggplot(data1, aes(x=hours,y=resids2)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

resids2.2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x=hours,y=resids2)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

resids3.2 <- ggplot(data3, aes(x=hours,y=resids2)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm")

plot1.2 + plot2.2 + plot3.2

```
## Residual plots

```{r}
resids1.2 + resids2.2 + resids3.2

```
